lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. Saturday, seven a.m., the hawker centre under Block 208.
**Auntie Rose:** Kavya! I must go to **Melaka** for my niece's wedding. Your family minds my stall this weekend, okay?
**Kavya:** Auntie Rose, we don't know how to make any of your drinks.
**Auntie Rose:** Easy! It's all on the recipe card. Just **keep it in proportion**! Bye!
**Dad:** A drinks stall. Two days. How hard can it be?
**Ah Boy:** I made bandung! **Four** cups of rose syrup and **one** cup of milk!
**Narrator:** But this documentary is about the tiny thing on the recipe card. Between the numbers.
**The Colonel:** The Colonel. I am the **ratio sign**. Two dots. One job: keeping numbers **in proportion**.
**The Colonel:** Syrup : milk = **1 : 4**. **One** part syrup for every **four** parts milk. Not four to one.
**The Colonel:** **Order. Matters.**
**Ah Boy:** It tastes nice, though.
**The Colonel:** Two days. One stall. Three amateurs. Nobody touches my ratios.
**Narrator:** Keep It in Proportion. Episode 7: Auntie Rose Goes to Melaka.
**The Colonel:** A **ratio** compares quantities of the **same kind**. Syrup to milk, **1 : 4**.
**Dad:** My jug: **250 ml** of syrup, **1 litre** of milk. So, **250 : 1**. Perfect.
**The Colonel:** **Same units first!** 1 litre = 1000 ml. So it's **250 : 1000**. Then drop the units.
**Chopper:** Chopper! I chop to **simplest form**! Divide every part by the **HCF**, 250! CHOP! **1 : 4**!
**Ah Boy:** Mine: **1.5** cups of syrup, **6** cups of milk. Right way round!
**The Colonel:** **No decimals.** Multiply both parts by 10: **15 : 60**.
**Chopper:** HCF fifteen! CHOP! **1 : 4**!
**Mum:** I used **½** a cup of syrup and **2** cups of milk.
**The Colonel:** **No fractions.** Multiply both parts by 2: **1 : 4**.
**Chopper:** Already simplest. Nothing to chop.
**The Colonel:** **Equivalent ratios.** Multiply or divide **every** part by the **same** number.
**Ah Boy:** So if I **add** one to both, **1 : 4** becomes **2 : 5**. Same drink?
**The Colonel:** No! **Adding** changes the ratio. **2 : 5** is far sweeter. **Out of proportion!**
**Narrator:** Ten a.m. 'Less sweet, please.' Mum and Dad compete.
**Dad:** Mine is **5 : 32**. Much less sweet.
**The Colonel:** Compare in the form **1 : n**. Divide **both** parts by the **first** part.
**Kavya:** Dad's has **less milk** for every part of syrup. Dad's is **sweeter**.
**Dad:** I was trying to make it **less** sweet.
**Narrator:** Two p.m. The tips jar holds **$84**.
**Priya:** Priya. Best friend. I worked **5** hours, Kavya **7**, Ah Boy **2**.
**Kavya:** So we share by hours. Ah Boy : Priya : Kavya = **2 : 5 : 7**.
**Ah Boy:** I worked 2 hours, so I get **84 ÷ 2 = $42**!
**Priya:** He worked the least and gets the most? I'm calling my lawyer.
**Barry:** Barry. **Bar model**. Never divide by **one** number in the ratio.
**Barry:** **Add** the parts: **2 + 5 + 7 = 14** boxes. All the same size. That's my whole personality.
**Barry:** **Divide**: 84 ÷ 14 = **$6** a box. Then **multiply** to build each share.
**Barry:** Check: 12 + 30 + 42 = **84**. Every dollar in a box.
**Ah Boy:** First add, then divide, then multiply. **A**h boy **D**eserves **M**ore.
**Narrator:** Four p.m. A cup-selling contest. Obviously.
**Priya:** Kavya and me: **7 : 4**. She sold **45** more cups than me.
**Barry:** Given the **difference**? Use the **difference in parts**: 7 − 4 = **3 parts** = 45 cups.
**Kavya:** And if you only knew Priya sold **60**? That's her **4 parts**. One part: **15** again.
**Priya:** Rematch. Tomorrow. Best of seven.
**Narrator:** Five p.m. Kavya's maths teacher, **Mr Tan**. He cannot stop teaching. Even on Saturdays.
**Mr Tan:** One kopi. Kavya: of today's bandung and lime juice, what fraction was bandung?
**Kavya:** Bandung : lime juice was **2 : 3**.
**Priya:** Easy! Bandung was **⅔** of the drinks.
**The Colonel:** **Out of proportion!**
**Barry:** Two boxes of bandung, three of lime. **2 + 3 = 5** boxes altogether.
**Mr Tan:** So bandung is **⅖** of the drinks and lime is **⅗**. Add the parts to get the denominator.
**Mr Tan:** **⅔** is **part to part**: two thirds **as many** bandung **as** lime. A different question.
**Mr Tan:** Backwards now. Your height is **⅘** of your dad's. Together you are **324 cm**.
**Kavya:** So me : Dad = **4 : 5**. **9 parts** = 324 cm, so one part is **36 cm**.
**Mr Tan:** I'd tell you a ratio joke, but you'd only get **two fifths** of it.
**Ah Boy:** I got zero fifths of it.
**Narrator:** Sunday. The board says **mango lassi: 3 cups for $10.50**. A man orders **7**.
**Dad:** Three cost ten fifty, so seven cost... how hard can it be?
**Uni:** Hi! I'm **Uni**! Uni means **one**! I'm the **unitary method**: find **ONE**, then find **ANY**!
**Kavya:** **Direct proportion**: double the cups, double the cost.
**Uni:** Cost ÷ cups is always **3.50**. That constant is **k**, so **y = 3.5x**.
**Uni:** On a graph: a **straight line through the origin**. Zero cups, zero dollars!
**Dad:** New idea! Lassi delivered to your flat, just a **$4** fee!
**Kavya:** Then **1** cup costs **$7.50** and **2** cups **$11**. That's not double.
**Uni:** The line misses the origin! A **fixed fee** breaks direct proportion.
**Dad:** Supermarket! **150 g** for **$1.20**. **500 g** for **$3.75**. **1 kg** for **$7.90**. Biggest is always cheapest.
**Uni:** Compare like with like: the **unit price**, per **100 g**.
**Kavya:** The **medium** wins: **lowest** price per 100 g. The biggest isn't always the best buy.
**Dad:** Three mediums. And I'm telling everyone it was my idea.

chapters.title: Lassi for six, and a kebaya

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Ten a.m. Auntie Rose's lassi recipe serves **4**. A family of **6** wants some.
**Priya:** Two more people? **Add 2** to everything!
**The Colonel:** Four mangoes. **502 g** of yoghurt. **202 ml** of milk. Out. Of. Proportion.
**Uni:** Never add! **Multiply** everything by the **multiplier**: new ÷ old = 6 ÷ 4 = **1.5**.
**Kavya:** **3** mangoes, **750 g** yoghurt, **300 ml** milk, **60 g** sugar.
**Narrator:** Eleven a.m. Make as many lassis as possible.
**Mum:** We have **7** mangoes, **1500 g** of yoghurt and **1 litre** of milk.
**Mum:** Yoghurt runs out first: the **limiting ingredient**. **3** batches, so 3 × 4 = **12** lassis.
**Dad:** It was the best buy. It just wasn't **enough** buy.
**Auntie Rose:** Kavya! The rate is **$1 = RM 3.40**. Auntie changed **$50**, got **RM 170**!
**Kavya:** Dollars to ringgit: **multiply**. 50 × 3.40 = **170**. Correct, Auntie.
**Auntie Rose:** Now this kebaya is **RM 85**. How much in dollars?
**Auntie Rose:** Two hundred and eighty-nine dollars?! For one kebaya?!
**Kavya:** Ringgit to dollars: **divide**. 85 ÷ 3.40 = **$25**. The ringgit number should be the **bigger** one.
**Auntie Rose:** Twenty-five! Then I'll buy two!
**Narrator:** One p.m. Kavya enlarges the menu on the photocopier.
**Kavya:** The menu is **4 cm by 6 cm**. I want the long side to be **15 cm**.
**Ah Boy:** 6 + 9 = 15, so add **9** to both sides: **13 cm by 15 cm**!
**The Colonel:** Squashed! Adding changes the **shape**. Out of proportion!
**Monty:** Monty. A **map**. On paper, small. In real life, **enormous**.
**Monty:** **Similar** shapes: same angles, and every length multiplied by the same **scale factor**, k.
**Monty:** Use **corresponding** sides, the long ones. k = new ÷ original = 15 ÷ 6 = **2.5**.
**Kavya:** Short side: 4 × 2.5 = **10 cm**. 4 : 6 = 2 : 3, and 10 : 15 = 2 : 3. Same shape!
**Narrator:** Two p.m. Auntie Rose is lost in Melaka.
**Auntie Rose:** My map says **1 : 50 000**. The hotel is **7 cm** away on the map. Can I walk?
**Monty:** 1 cm on the map is **50 000 cm** in real life. Same units on both sides.
**Monty:** Map to real: **multiply**. 7 × 50 000 = **350 000 cm**.
**Kavya:** ÷ 100: **3500 m**. ÷ 1000: **3.5 km**. In a kebaya, Auntie? Take a trishaw.
**Auntie Rose:** Tomorrow's trishaw tour is **6 km**. How long is that on my map?
**Kavya:** Real to map: **cm first**. 6 km = **600 000 cm**. Then **divide**: 600 000 ÷ 50 000 = **12 cm**.
**Monty:** **Real world is huge: multiply. Map is tiny: divide.**
**Auntie Rose:** Six kilometres. My poor trishaw uncle.
**Narrator:** Sunday, nine p.m. Closing time. A mountain of cups.
**Mum:** With **6** of us washing, it takes **10 minutes**. Mr Tan came back for a third kopi.
**Dad:** Mum and I are going upstairs. How long for the other **4**?
**Ivy:** Ivy. **Inverse proportion**. When one quantity goes **up**, the other goes **down**.
**Ivy:** **Fewer** people, **more** time. Expect more than 10 minutes.
**Ivy:** The **product** stays the same: 6 × 10 = **60** person-minutes.
**Kavya:** So **4** people take 60 ÷ 4 = **15 minutes**.
**Ivy:** **x × y = 60**, so **y = 60 ÷ x**. My curve gets closer to the axes, but **never touches**.
**Ivy:** Personal space.
**Mr Tan:** Washing up: inverse proportion, with bubbles.
**Priya:** I'll **sing**! **Twice** the singers, **half** the time!
**Ivy:** No. Some things aren't proportional at all. Twice the singers, same song. Just louder.
**Auntie Rose:** Kavya! Coach stuck in traffic! Usually **80 km/h** for **3 hours**. Tonight, only **60 km/h**!
**Ivy:** Slower, so **longer**. Speed × time = 80 × 3 = **240 km**. 240 ÷ 60 = **4 hours**.

chapters.title: The stall saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the stall would like to save you some marks.
**The Colonel:** One. **Order matters.** Boys : girls is not girls : boys.
**Dad:** Two. **Same units first.** 50 cm : 2 m is **1 : 4**. Ask me how I know.
**Ah Boy:** Three. Divide by the **total** number of parts, not one number in the ratio. I gave the money back.
**Barry:** Four. Given the **difference**? Use the **difference in parts**, not the total.
**Monty:** Five. **1 km = 100 000 cm.** Every. Single. Time.
**Auntie Rose:** Six. Currency: **check** which number should be bigger. Auntie nearly paid two hundred and eighty-nine dollars.
**Narrator:** Keep It in Proportion will return.
**Narrator:** Monday, six a.m. Auntie Rose is back.
**Auntie Rose:** Stall still standing. Very good. Who made this pink one?
**Ah Boy:** Me! **Four** parts syrup, **one** part milk!
**Auntie Rose:** Wah. Going on the menu. **Ah Boy Special**. Six dollars.
**The Colonel:** Order... matters...
